herodotus.author: Herodotus
herodotus.note: main narrative; wrote about 50 years after the battle, from Athenian and other informants

aeschylus.author: Aeschylus
aeschylus.note: a play staged 8 years after the battle, for an audience of men who fought in it

morrison.author: J. S. Morrison, J. F. Coates and N. B. Rankov

athlit.author: L. Casson and J. R. Steffy (eds.)

facts.claim: The battle of Salamis was fought in 480 BC, traditionally dated to late September.
Before the invasion, Athenian envoys at Delphi received a terrifying first answer from the priestess Aristonice: flee to the ends of the earth.
The envoys returned as suppliants carrying olive branches and were given a second answer: Zeus grants that a wooden wall alone shall not be taken.
The second answer also said: divine Salamis, you will destroy the children of women.
Some older Athenians believed the wooden wall meant the thorn hedge that once ringed the Acropolis.
Others said the wooden wall meant the ships, and Themistocles argued the oracle would have said 'cruel Salamis', not 'divine', if Athenians were meant to die there.
The Athenians decided to meet the invader at sea with their ships, together with the other Greeks who were willing.
Years earlier Themistocles had persuaded Athens to spend a rich new silver strike from the Laurium mines on warships instead of sharing the money out.

facts.note: Herodotus says 200 ships; Plutarch and Aristotle's Constitution of the Athenians say 100. Say 'a new fleet' or give both numbers.
facts.claim: Herodotus says the silver built 200 ships.
The Athenians evacuated their families and slaves to Troezen, Aegina and Salamis.
A few Athenians, the temple stewards and poor men, stayed on the Acropolis behind a barricade of planks and timber, believing it was the wooden wall of the oracle.
The Persians climbed the steep front of the Acropolis near the shrine of Aglauros, where no guard was posted.
They killed the defenders, plundered the temple and set the whole Acropolis on fire.
Xerxes sent a horseman to Susa to announce his success.

facts.note: A story the Athenians told Herodotus; say 'Herodotus says' or 'the Athenians said'.
facts.claim: Herodotus says Athena's sacred olive tree burned with the temple, yet the next day a new shoot a cubit long had grown from the stump.
When news reached the Greek fleet at Salamis that the Acropolis had fallen, some commanders panicked and voted to sail away to the Isthmus.
Athens supplied the largest contingent of the Greek fleet: 180 ships.
Themistocles sent the message when he was losing the council debate to the Peloponnesian commanders, who wanted to leave Salamis and fight at the Isthmus.
Sicinnus was a slave of Themistocles' household and the tutor of his children.
Themistocles sent him by boat to the Persian commanders with a message: Themistocles was on the king's side, and the Greeks were terrified and planning to flee.
The message said that if the Persians stopped the Greeks escaping, they would see them fighting among themselves.
Aeschylus, eight years later, also tells of a Greek who came to Xerxes saying the Greeks would slip away under cover of night.
The Persians believed it: that night they moved their ships to close the channels around Salamis and landed soldiers on the islet of Psyttaleia.
Aristides, Themistocles' old rival who had been ostracised from Athens, crossed from Aegina and brought word that the fleet was surrounded.
Afterwards Themistocles made Sicinnus a citizen of Thespiae and a rich man.
Modern historians read the message as a deliberate trap to force the battle into the narrow strait.
Xerxes watched the battle seated at the foot of Mount Aigaleos, on the mainland opposite Salamis.
Whenever he saw one of his captains do something notable, he asked who it was, and his scribes wrote down the captain's name, his father and his city.
Plutarch says Xerxes sat on a golden throne, with many secretaries beside him to record the battle.
Artemisia, queen of Halicarnassus, chased by an Athenian ship, rammed and sank a ship from her own side.
Xerxes thought she had sunk a Greek ship and said: my men have become women, and my women men.
When Phoenician captains blamed the Ionians for the defeat, Xerxes had them beheaded.
Aeschylus says that when Xerxes saw the depth of the disaster he tore his robes and cried out, for he had a seat in full view of the whole army, on a high hill near the sea.
A trireme's main weapon was a bronze ram fixed at the waterline of its bow.
A trireme carried about 170 rowers on three levels and about 200 men in all.
Herodotus says the Athenian Ameinias of Pallene was the first to ram an enemy ship; when the ships locked together, others came to help and the battle began.
Aeschylus says a Greek ship began the ramming and smashed off the curved stern of a Phoenician ship.
In the narrow strait the crowded Persian ships could not use their numbers; they struck each other with their bronze rams and broke their oars.

facts.note: Herodotus gives 378 Greek ships; modern historians think the Persian fleet was far smaller than 1,207 by the day of battle. Say 'Aeschylus claims'.
facts.claim: Aeschylus puts the Greek fleet at about 310 ships and Xerxes' fleet at 1,207.

The largest ancient warship ram ever found, the Athlit ram, was discovered off Israel in 1980: one piece of cast bronze, about 2.26 metres long and 465 kilograms. It comes from a later warship, not from Salamis.
